title: Ironbank Financial - Security review (RBAC, SSO/SAML, audit logs)
summary: Enterprise security review with Ironbank Financial covering Redwood’s RBAC v2 direction (least privilege, scoped role bindings, deny-by-default), SSO/SAML integration and group-to-role mapping expectations, and audit logging requirements for evidence and SIEM ingestion. Ironbank requested concrete examples: permission catalog granularity, audit event schema including authorization decision context, and operational controls like break-glass access + review. Redwood clarified hosted vs dedicated vs private semantics and current roadmap/timing for RBAC v2 rollout and migration compatibility.
topics: RBAC v2 model: permissions, role templates, scopes (org/project/env/cluster)
Deny-by-default enforcement and where checks occur (gateway vs service)
SSO/SAML and IdP group mapping, separation of duties
Audit logging: event coverage, retention, export to SIEM, authz decision fields
Evidence expectations for SOC2 / customer questionnaire
Private deployment considerations (customer-managed networking, log export paths)
action_items: Redwood (Kevin Osei): Send a redacted sample audit log event showing authz decision context (allow/deny, permission string, scope, policy version, denial reason code) by 2025-02-24
Redwood (Marcus Lin): Share RBAC v2 security FAQ + permission naming convention excerpt (what is stable, deprecation/versioning) by 2025-02-24
Redwood (Kaitlyn Nguyen): Confirm SAML SSO setup details (supported claims, group mapping approach, SCIM status) and send implementation notes by 2025-02-25
Ironbank (Mike Hargrove): Provide IdP details (Okta/AAD, group claim format, expected RBAC scopes) and preferred “break-glass” process constraints by 2025-02-26
Redwood (Colin O'Donnell): Schedule follow-up technical deep dive on policy evaluation/caching + latency impact with Ironbank platform team by 2025-02-27
Ironbank (Elena Ruiz): Share their vendor evidence checklist (SOC2 artifacts, pen test, SDLC controls) for Redwood to map against by 2025-02-26
next_steps: Redwood to send sample audit log + SIEM mapping notes (Splunk-style fields) and RBAC v2 documentation links
Ironbank to validate whether org/project/environment scope model fits their internal separation-of-duties policy
Book a 60-min deep dive with Ironbank IAM + SOC teams focused on audit export + incident investigation workflow
If scope model aligns, identify 1–2 pilot workflows (audit export, key rotation, routing policy edits) to validate least-privilege roles
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-02-20
Time: 3:00pm - 3:58pm ET
Duration: 58 minutes
Call type: Security / compliance review
Account: Ironbank Financial

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Colin O'Donnell, Marcus Lin, Naomi Feldman, Kevin Osei, Kaitlyn Nguyen
Ironbank Financial: Sonia Patel (Security Arch), Mike Hargrove (IAM), Elena Ruiz (GRC), Arjun Mehta (Platform), Tom Nguyen (SOC)

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Customer asked for least-privilege RBAC with provable enforcement, SAML SSO, and detailed audit logs exported to SIEM.
- Redwood described RBAC v2: permission catalog, role templates, scoped bindings, deny-by-default checks at gateway + services.
- Customer requested evidence artifacts: sample audit log events, SOC2 report, controls, and how denial reasons are shown.


Transcript

[00:00] Colin O'Donnell: Alright, I think we’re at time. Thanks everybody for joining. This is Colin from Redwood. We’ve got Marcus from Security Eng, Naomi our PM on security controls, Kevin on audit logging/export, and Kaitlyn who owns authn/authz integration.

[00:14] Sonia Patel: Great. Thanks, Colin. This is Sonia, security architecture. Mike is our IAM lead. Elena from GRC. Arjun from platform engineering. Tom from the SOC.

[00:24] Colin O'Donnell: Perfect. The agenda we had: RBAC, SSO—SAML specifically—then audit logging, what you need for evidence, and we’ll end with next steps. Does that still work?

[00:35] Sonia Patel: Yep. And just to set context, we’re evaluating both dedicated capacity and potentially a private deployment later. But for the security review we want to understand what’s true across all of those.

[00:47] Naomi Feldman: That makes sense. We’ve been aligning semantics across hosted, dedicated, and private so it’s a consistent story.

[00:55] Colin O'Donnell: Cool. Sonia, do you want to kick off with your top questions, or should we go through our checklist?

[01:02] Sonia Patel: Let’s do top questions. One, do you have least privilege RBAC, like not just admin/user. Two, can we tie access to our IdP groups via SAML. Three, audit logs—do they show who did what, and also “who tried to do what and got denied.” And then evidence—we get asked to provide samples, retention, and export to SIEM.

[01:25] Marcus Lin: Got it. I’ll start with RBAC. We have an RBAC v2 initiative, which is basically moving from coarse roles to explicit permission strings that are checked in a deny-by-default way. The model is: permissions, roles which are sets of permissions, and role bindings that attach roles to identities at a scope.

[01:44] Mike Hargrove: Scope meaning like project or environment, not just org?

[01:48] Marcus Lin: Exactly. Org is the top-level. Then we have projects—sometimes customers call those workspaces—and then environments within a project. For private deployments there’s also cluster scoping because you might have multiple runtime clusters.

[02:04] Arjun Mehta: Okay. We care about separating duties. Like, a platform operator can manage routing policy or model pinning, but cannot export audit logs. And our security admins can export logs and manage keys, but can’t change inference routing.

[02:18] Naomi Feldman: That’s aligned with how we’re designing the role templates. We typically propose separate roles like “Security Admin”, “Deployment Operator”, “Read-only Auditor”, plus “Org Admin” which is the superset but you’d restrict.

[02:33] Elena Ruiz: When you say “templates,” are those fixed? Or can we make custom roles?

[02:38] Naomi Feldman: You can do both. We provide built-in templates as a starting point, and you can define custom roles by selecting permissions. For regulated customers we see templates + small deltas.

[02:51] Sonia Patel: What’s the granularity of permissions? Like, is it “manage audit logs” or is it “export audit logs” vs “view audit logs.”

[02:59] Kevin Osei: It’s broken down. For audit, we’re separating view/search from export, and export includes destination config. And we separate “configure retention” from “export.”

[03:12] Tom Nguyen: From SOC perspective, we need to know if someone changes retention, that’s a big deal. So yes, separate permission.

[03:18] Kevin Osei: Yep. That’s exactly the intent.

[03:23] Mike Hargrove: And enforcement wise, where is it actually checked? Like is it in the UI only? Because we don’t accept “front end check.”

[03:31] Marcus Lin: Totally fair. Enforcement is on the server side. We check permissions at the API gateway for most request paths, and then services enforce as well for sensitive operations. The idea is defense in depth.

[03:45] Kaitlyn Nguyen: And we’re moving to a standardized annotation model so endpoints declare the permission they require, and we have CI tests to prevent shipping a sensitive endpoint without an authz annotation. That’s part of the “provable enforcement” story.

[04:03] Sonia Patel: Is deny-by-default actually on? Or is it a roadmap?

[04:07] Marcus Lin: For v2, yes, it’s deny-by-default. During migration we run dual-read: we evaluate v1 and v2 in parallel and compare decisions, but enforcement can be feature-flagged per environment or tenant. The end state is v2 is the source of truth and anything not explicitly allowed is denied.

[04:28] Arjun Mehta: We’ve seen vendors say “deny-by-default” but then there are implicit admin bypasses.

[04:33] Marcus Lin: We’re trying to keep implicit permissions minimal. There is a break-glass process for emergencies, but it’s time-bound and audited. It’s not a silent bypass.

[04:44] Tom Nguyen: Break-glass meaning you can elevate to admin in prod.

[04:48] Marcus Lin: Yes, but it’s approval-based. Fiona on our SecOps team monitors that. And the event is captured with who approved, start/end, and what actions were taken during elevation.

[05:02] Elena Ruiz: Is that available for customer admins too? Or just Redwood internal?

[05:06] Naomi Feldman: For hosted, the break-glass flow is primarily for Redwood internal operational access, and customer admins use normal RBAC. For private deployments, customers can set their own operational procedures, but we provide patterns and logging hooks.

[05:23] Sonia Patel: Okay. Let’s talk SSO. We’re SAML to Okta. We want groups to map to roles.

[05:30] Kaitlyn Nguyen: We support SAML SSO, and we can map IdP group claims to roles at org scope or narrower scopes depending on your setup. Some customers do “Okta group -> Redwood role template.”

[05:45] Mike Hargrove: Is it true group mapping or do we have to manually assign users in the console.

[05:49] Kaitlyn Nguyen: For enterprise deployments we support group-based role assignment, so you don’t have to do per-user click ops. There are some constraints based on what your IdP sends in the SAML assertion. We can walk through the claim format.

[06:06] Mike Hargrove: We usually send groups as a list, but it can be huge. We typically use a filtered attribute.

[06:12] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Right, and we usually recommend a dedicated “Redwood-*” group naming convention and filter on that.

[06:19] Sonia Patel: Do you support SCIM for provisioning?

[06:22] Kaitlyn Nguyen: For user lifecycle, we have SCIM on the roadmap for broader rollout; some customers are in early access. For the near term, SAML + JIT provisioning and group-to-role mapping covers access control. We can confirm timelines offline.

[06:40] Elena Ruiz: For evidence, we will need what exact attributes you require from SAML and what you store.

[06:46] Kaitlyn Nguyen: We can provide an integration guide, including the assertion fields we consume, and we log SSO events.

[06:54] Kevin Osei: And those SSO login events can be part of the audit trail as well.

[07:00] Tom Nguyen: Okay, audit logs. What do you log, where do the logs live, and can we export to Splunk.

[07:07] Kevin Osei: We emit audit events for security-relevant actions across console and API: auth events, API key management, role/role binding changes, routing policy modifications, model pinning/rollouts, private deployment admin actions, data retention config, and audit export config itself.

[07:28] Sonia Patel: Do you include “read” operations? Like someone viewing an API key list.

[07:33] Kevin Osei: For highly sensitive reads, yes. For general reads, it depends—there’s a balance between signal and noise. But viewing/exporting audit logs, changing roles, creating tokens/keys—those are always logged. We can share our coverage list at a high level.

[07:51] Marcus Lin: Also, in RBAC v2 we add authorization decision context into the audit logs. So not just “action happened,” but the authorization evaluation: subject, permission required, scope, allow/deny, and if denied, a reason code.

[08:10] Tom Nguyen: That’s big for us. We want denied attempts in the SIEM.

[08:14] Kevin Osei: Yes. We can log both allowed and denied checks for a subset of sensitive actions. There is some tuning because you don’t want to flood logs with every single denied request like a UI polling.

[08:27] Arjun Mehta: Right, otherwise Splunk costs go brr.

[08:30] Kevin Osei: Exactly. So we focus on enforcement points and sensitive routes. We can also sample, but for your compliance requirements we can pin a stricter policy.

[08:43] Sonia Patel: What’s in the authz decision fields exactly?

[08:46] Kevin Osei: Typically: actor (user ID, email if available), authn method (SSO/API key/service token), action/permission string, resource identifiers, scope (org/project/env/cluster), policy version hash, decision allow/deny, and denial reason code. We also capture request metadata like IP, user agent for console.

[09:09] Elena Ruiz: And retention? For regulated we do 365 days.

[09:13] Kevin Osei: Default retention varies by plan; for enterprise we can support longer retention. For private deployments you can set retention to your own storage backend.

[09:23] Sonia Patel: “Set retention” meaning you actually have a control in the product.

[09:27] Naomi Feldman: Yes, we’re adding explicit retention controls that are permissioned. So a billing admin can’t modify it; a security admin can.

[09:38] Mike Hargrove: How do you export audit logs. Is it API pull, push, or both.

[09:44] Kevin Osei: Today we support export APIs and scheduled exports. For enterprise we commonly set up: S3-compatible bucket export, webhook to a collector, or direct integration via our audit-log exporter service that formats fields for SIEMs.

[10:02] Tom Nguyen: If we’re dedicated or private, can we ship logs to our Splunk HEC.

[10:06] Kevin Osei: For private, yes, you can configure a log forwarder in your environment. For dedicated, we can push to your endpoint or you pull via API depending on network rules.

[10:20] Sonia Patel: We’ll need a sample event. Like an example of “user tried to export logs but got denied.”

[10:25] Kevin Osei: We can provide a redacted JSON example after the call.

[10:30] Elena Ruiz: Also, we need to confirm you meet SOC 2. Do you have a current report?

[10:35] Marcus Lin: Yes, we have SOC 2 Type II. We can share the report under NDA via your portal.

[10:43] Elena Ruiz: Great. And we’ll ask about pen tests, vulnerability management, SDLC controls.

[10:49] Marcus Lin: Understood. We’ll map to your evidence checklist once you send it.

[10:54] Colin O'Donnell: Just to make sure we’re hitting what you need: you’re evaluating dedicated now, and private later, and you want RBAC and audit logs to be consistent.

[11:04] Sonia Patel: Correct. Also, separation of duties. Specifically: platform team can manage “inference routing” but not IAM; security team can manage IAM but not product configuration.

[11:18] Naomi Feldman: That’s a common enterprise requirement. In RBAC v2 we explicitly have permissions for “routing policies: create/update/delete,” “model rollout: start/cancel/approve,” and those are separate from “org: manage users/roles,” “keys: rotate,” “audit: export.”

[11:39] Arjun Mehta: And what about API keys. We want keys scoped to project if possible.

[11:45] Kaitlyn Nguyen: We support scoped API keys—project-scoped keys—so a key used by a service can’t touch org-level admin actions. And in v2, key permissions are enforced similarly.

[12:01] Mike Hargrove: Can a key call admin endpoints at all.

[12:05] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Only if you explicitly bind a role that includes admin permissions to that service identity. Default is no.

[12:14] Sonia Patel: Good. Another question: can you explain “why denied” to the user. We have helpdesk tickets where users get 403 and no clue.

[12:23] Naomi Feldman: We’re adding structured denial reason codes. End users get a safe message: “missing permission X at scope Y.” Admins can optionally see more detail in a debug header or in the console’s permission viewer.

[12:39] Tom Nguyen: Please don’t leak sensitive policy logic.

[12:42] Marcus Lin: Agreed. Denial reasons are curated. We differentiate what’s shown to normal users vs org admins.

[12:51] Arjun Mehta: When you say debug header—like in the API response.

[12:55] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Optional header, gated. You’d enable it for admins or in a support session.

[13:03] Sonia Patel: Okay. Let’s talk about private deployment quickly. If we install in our VPC, do we still hit your control plane for auth.

[13:12] Colin O'Donnell: For private, there’s a private control plane option. You can run the control plane in your environment, and policies are evaluated locally. There’s still an update channel for software updates, but authorization decisions don’t have to transit our SaaS.

[13:29] Arjun Mehta: And for performance—policy checks won’t add latency to inference calls.

[13:35] Marcus Lin: For inference generation endpoints, we keep the authz check lightweight and cacheable. The goal is microseconds to a couple milliseconds. We cache policy evaluation results with safe TTL and invalidate on role changes.

[13:52] Tom Nguyen: Cache invalidation is always where it breaks. How do you ensure it’s correct.

[13:58] Marcus Lin: Two parts: scope-correct cache keys (org/project/env) and explicit invalidation events on role/role binding changes. Also short TTLs as a safety backstop. And metrics to detect stale decision mismatches.

[14:15] Sonia Patel: Do you log policy version in the audit log.

[14:19] Kevin Osei: Yes, policy bundle version hash, so you can correlate decisions to the policy state at the time.

[14:27] Elena Ruiz: That helps for evidence.

[14:31] Mike Hargrove: For SAML, do you support step-up auth or MFA.

[14:36] Kaitlyn Nguyen: We defer to your IdP for MFA. So if Okta enforces MFA for certain apps/groups, Redwood inherits that.

[14:46] Mike Hargrove: Makes sense.

[14:48] Sonia Patel: What about local accounts. Can we disable password login.

[14:53] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Yes, SSO-only mode is supported for enterprise. You can restrict or disable local auth.

[15:02] Tom Nguyen: One more on audit logs: do you include source IP and user agent.

[15:06] Kevin Osei: For console actions, yes. For API actions, we log IP as observed at the gateway. For private, depends on your ingress, but we can capture x-forwarded-for if configured.

[15:22] Sonia Patel: And time sync and timestamps. Are they UTC.

[15:26] Kevin Osei: Stored in UTC with ISO timestamps.

[15:30] Elena Ruiz: Can you provide data residency options.

[15:34] Colin O'Donnell: For dedicated/private, yes. For hosted we have regional options, and we can align logging storage with region depending on plan.

[15:46] Sonia Patel: Okay. I want to understand what’s shipping now vs in-progress. You mentioned RBAC v2. Is it GA.

[15:55] Naomi Feldman: It’s in phased rollout. Some enterprise tenants are in pilot. The permission catalog and enforcement middleware are in place for critical endpoints; we’re finishing coverage across remaining control plane routes and console admin flows. Migration is feature-flagged with dual-read until we’re confident.

[16:16] Arjun Mehta: If we start dedicated next month, will we be on v2.

[16:21] Naomi Feldman: We can plan that. We usually start with v1 compatibility mode and enable v2 per workflow. For your needs, we can prioritize enabling v2 for the admin/security sensitive actions first.

[16:34] Sonia Patel: I’d like that. We don’t want surprises where an endpoint isn’t protected yet.

[16:40] Marcus Lin: Understood. We can share our coverage statement: which endpoint families are v2 enforced, and which are still in migration.

[16:51] Elena Ruiz: That coverage statement is important for our risk committee.

[16:56] Colin O'Donnell: Noted. We’ll put it in writing.

[17:01] Mike Hargrove: On group mapping, can we do group -> role binding at project scope. Like “LLM-ProjectA-Operators.”

[17:10] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Yes, that’s the pattern. You define the role binding at the project scope. The group is mapped to that binding.

[17:19] Mike Hargrove: Okay. And if the same user is in multiple groups, do they get union of permissions.

[17:25] Marcus Lin: Yes, additive. Unless there’s an explicit deny concept—currently we’re not exposing customer-configurable denies in v2. So it’s the union of allowed permissions.

[17:40] Sonia Patel: No explicit deny is okay as long as templates are clean. We can keep groups separate.

[17:47] Tom Nguyen: For SIEM, can you map to a common schema. Like actor, action, outcome.

[17:53] Kevin Osei: Yes, we have an exporter that maps to a normalized schema: event.action, event.outcome (success/failure), user.name, source.ip, and then Redwood-specific fields like redwood.permission, redwood.scope. We can provide that mapping.

[18:12] Tom Nguyen: Great.

[18:14] Elena Ruiz: Also we need the contract language around audit log retention and availability.

[18:20] Colin O'Donnell: That’s typically in the enterprise order form and addendum. We can loop in our legal after we get through technical fit.

[18:28] Sonia Patel: Okay. Can we go a bit deeper on “permission strings.” Do you have a naming convention. We hate ad hoc.

[18:36] Marcus Lin: Yes, we standardized: namespace.resource.verb style, like org.user.manage or audit.export.create. That’s not the exact string but that flavor. And we version/deprecate in a controlled way to avoid breaking policies.

[18:55] Arjun Mehta: And you won’t rename them every quarter.

[18:58] Marcus Lin: Right. Permission identifiers are treated as API surface. We deprecate with a timeline.

[19:05] Sonia Patel: Okay. How about “routing policy edits”—what’s the scope. Is it per environment.

[19:12] Naomi Feldman: Typically per environment because routing policy affects deployed traffic. But there are org-level guardrails. In dedicated/private you may also have cluster-level routing config.

[19:28] Arjun Mehta: That matches our mental model.

[19:31] Tom Nguyen: On denied attempts, do you include reason codes. Like missing permission vs invalid scope.

[19:37] Kevin Osei: Yes. Missing permission, missing binding at scope, expired session, policy evaluation error, and a few others. Policy evaluation errors are treated as deny and alert.

[19:52] Sonia Patel: If your policy engine is down, do you fail open.

[19:56] Marcus Lin: No. Fail closed. Deny-by-default and fail-closed.

[20:03] Sonia Patel: Good.

[20:04] Colin O'Donnell: Maybe let’s pause and see if there are any other big security items outside RBAC/audit.

[20:11] Elena Ruiz: Not for today. But we will send the evidence list.

[20:15] Mike Hargrove: Just one: do you support session timeout controls.

[20:19] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Yes, admin-configurable session duration and re-auth requirements for sensitive actions is on the roadmap; today we have baseline session controls and rely on SSO policies.

[20:33] Sonia Patel: Okay.

[20:35] Arjun Mehta: I want to ask about “who can change roles.” We want that restricted to a small security admin group.

[20:42] Naomi Feldman: Role and role binding management is permissioned separately. So you can allow a security admin group to manage that, and platform operators won’t have that permission.

[20:54] Arjun Mehta: And can an org admin create a role that gives themselves everything.

[20:59] Marcus Lin: If someone is an org admin, yes they can escalate by definition. That’s why we recommend minimizing org admins and using specific admin roles. For private deployments you can also do additional controls like require two-person review for certain actions, but that’s a separate feature.

[21:17] Sonia Patel: Understood.

[21:18] Tom Nguyen: For incident investigations, can we search logs by actor and by resource.

[21:24] Kevin Osei: Yes, in console and API. In private you can also do it directly in your log store.

[21:32] Sonia Patel: Okay. I think the main deliverables we need are the sample audit log, the RBAC permission naming and coverage, and the SAML group mapping doc.

[21:44] Colin O'Donnell: Great. We can do that.

[21:47] Naomi Feldman: And if you want, we can also share a draft role template set. Like: Security Admin, Auditor, Platform Operator, Billing Admin. So you can sanity check separation of duties.

[22:00] Sonia Patel: Yes, please.

[22:02] Elena Ruiz: And can you state what’s in audit logs for RBAC changes. Like create role, change binding.

[22:08] Kevin Osei: Those are fully logged: before/after diff, actor, timestamp, scope.

[22:16] Tom Nguyen: With allow/deny context.

[22:18] Kevin Osei: For the action itself, it’s an allowed action so yes, it includes the authorization context. And if someone tries and is denied, that attempt can be logged too.

[22:31] Mike Hargrove: Another minor point: we need SAML cert rotation process.

[22:36] Kaitlyn Nguyen: We support rotating IdP certificates. We can document the procedure.

[22:42] Sonia Patel: Great.

[22:44] Colin O'Donnell: Can we talk about timeline. You mentioned next month for dedicated. Are you aiming March.

[22:50] Arjun Mehta: Our internal target is end of March for a small pilot.

[22:55] Colin O'Donnell: Great. We can do a follow-up technical deep dive next week on policy evaluation/caching and private deployment options, and parallel we’ll send the evidence docs.

[23:08] Sonia Patel: Works.

[23:10] Fireflies.ai: (crosstalk)

[23:11] Tom Nguyen: Sorry, one last. Do you support alerting on break-glass usage.

[23:16] Marcus Lin: Yes. Break-glass triggers alerts to SecOps internally, and for private you can wire that to your alerting system as well.

[23:24] Tom Nguyen: Cool.

[23:25] Sonia Patel: Okay, I’m good.

[23:27] Colin O'Donnell: Great. Let’s do quick recap and next steps.

[23:31] Colin O'Donnell: Redwood will send: (1) redacted sample audit log events including authz decision fields and denial reason codes, plus SIEM mapping; (2) RBAC v2 overview, permission naming/versioning, and role template matrix; (3) SAML group mapping setup guide including attributes and cert rotation; and (4) a coverage note on which endpoint families are currently v2 enforced vs in migration.

[23:58] Colin O'Donnell: Ironbank will send: your evidence checklist and some details on Okta group claim format and desired scope model, plus any constraints on break-glass and separation of duties.

[24:10] Sonia Patel: Yep.

[24:11] Colin O'Donnell: We’ll schedule a deep dive with Arjun and Mike, likely 60 minutes, focusing on policy evaluation locality, caching TTL/invalidation, and any private deployment questions.

[24:22] Arjun Mehta: Sounds good.

[24:24] Elena Ruiz: Thank you.

[24:25] Colin O'Donnell: Thanks all.

[24:27] Fireflies.ai: Meeting ended.

Note: Transcript ended early due to recorder stopping; remaining discussion (approx. 30+ minutes) continued off-record according to participants. Redwood follow-up notes indicate additional Q&A on retention SLAs and SOC2 evidence sharing via NDA.
